First, I believe that the statement that the NRC was limiting its basic research came from some external advisers. The hon. member knows perfectly well that in any sound business, and indeed any government agency, work does not continue on and on without reviewing, exploring, and having an in-depth study of the programs and mandate. Perhaps these were external researchers who were getting this type of information.
I can assure you that Dr. Perron, the president of the NRC, states that the commitment of the NRC is to basic research in priority areas. They are not going to change that mandate. Their priority areas include legally mandated areas such as astronomy, standards in measurements research, as well as the basic research needed to maintain skills in generic research programs. This has been NRC's fundamental role in basic research for some time as it focuses upon long term applied research with broad applications to industry and government programs.
Universities play an important role in basic research and the government is supporting this activity through the granting councils and the Centres of Excellence program. We have the Medical Granting Council as well as NSRC. There are three major ones. They do tremendous work. You do not put all your funding into one area. Regardless, basic research at the NRC will not only be maintained but it will be strengthened, as I said earlier in my speech, by collaboration with other performers in universities and research organizations.
The NRC, in fact, as a collaborator in 10 of the 14 chosen networks surely shows its importance and why those new centres will come forth and bring benefits to this country, not just tomorrow, but long term benefits.
The hon. member did question me on privatization and divestiture. I thought that I heard the parliamentary secretary state that our National Research Council will not be privatized. The NRC internal working memo refers to privatization and divestiture and it clearly states the NRC is going to encourage private consortia to assist in its operations and its facilities, but it will not be privatizing.
It is time that we became involved in partnerships. We cannot remain stagnant. It is very important to realize that just because money has been spent in one area for the past five or ten years, there are certainly no criteria or guidelines to suggest that the money should continue to be spent in that way.
Dr. Perron and the NRC's five-year program will show us the direction of Canada and why we have to become more competitive, and why research and development is so important, not just for the federal and provincial governments, but for universities and private industries.
It was interesting yesterday at the standing committee meeting. Dr. May from NSERC appeared before us and explained the good things that NSERC is doing and how their budget has been maintained, and indeed increased. That gets back to my concluding statement that although elementary and secondary education falls within the

jurisdiction of the provinces, somehow-and I do not have the magic answer-we have to stimulate young people to be interested, to be inquisitive and to want to grasp the sciences and to go into engineering and to our science portfolios.

Mr. Speaker, when I was 18 and just leaving high school, the very first job I applied for was at the National Research Council. I had no idea then that I would be standing here all these years later fighting a battle to preserve that institution. One of the proudest moments of my life was when I was accepted for a job in hot and cold state physics at the National Research Council.
I had grown up with the view of this institution epitomizing Canada's excellence in fields of research that were not happening anywhere else in the world, epitomizing our progress and adventurous spirit and our high stature, despite the fact that we were such a small country.
Things changed that summer, and I ended up going back to university and eventually making other decisions about the course of my life. Otherwise, I might have been sitting in the gallery today wondering what my fate was going to be instead of standing here defending those people who have made this country great and created our reputation internationally and continue to do so, despite the hammering that they have received at the hands of this government.
I want to talk about the people. The new frontiers of human endeavour are no longer the frontiers of geography, distance and climate. They are the frontiers of the human mind. We only conquer those frontiers and go beyond them with people of courage, commitment and dedication who are prepared to work for years and sometimes for decades with no specific results, except the pursuit of a new idea that eventually will lead somewhere. I will come back to that theme. I want to talk a little more about how the people who have done this for the country are being treated.
Government Orders
Aside from the cut-backs, aside from the people who are leaving-and they are now in the hundreds-the people who have been forced, coerced or cajoled into leaving are lost to us as a nation, not just to the National Research Council. As a nation these people are lost to us. The whole atmosphere has been demoralizing.
Mr. Perron writes one thing, and then he sends an internal memo to employees which states something else. On the one hand, he reaffirms to the employees the commitment to excellence and basic research. On the other hand, in another document he states: "We will be trimming our basic research to the bare minimum necessary for a minimal insurance policy", whatever the heck that means.
He talks about planned partnerships and working with others in his memo to the employees, and then in another memo talks about planned partnerships as the driving force behind the National Research Council. Planned partnerships are not a driving force, they are not an objective or a mission for an organization. They are tools to accomplish certain things. But to say something like that is to be the driving force is absolutely ridiculous.
It is no wonder people are demoralized, wondering where their life's work is going and wondering where there careers are going. They are being treated inhumanely as employees. There is an unofficial attrition program at the National Research Council that is far more vicious than many of the formal ones taking place in the public service. People are unprotected. They are obviously being hushed up when they retire early. We have statements and numerous clippings over the last three years which indicate that people are not free to comment. Why are we buying off people? People who have dedicated their lives to this country deserve decent treatment when they leave.
The most important thing is that scientists are being prevented from speaking out about what they and they alone know. What is wrong with free and open examination in the media of the implications of the actions of the government in cutting millions of dollars from the budget of the prime institution of basic research in this country?
There was a memorandum sent to the employees of the National Research Council which stated:
March 16, 1990

Government Orders
In the current climate, it is preferable to limit the number of people
speaking on behalf of NRC.
Contrary to the policy that scientists are free to speak out on their areas of expertise, the memo states: "If a reporter calls you, please do not answer", instead call the head of the communications section. That is stifling and gagging people. The very people who should be front and centre in the debate about the future of the National Research Council, because it is fundamental to the future of science in this country, are being told they cannot speak out.
Good research is done by teams of people. These teams take time to assemble. They can be broken up quickly, but they cannot be rebuilt quickly. The actions that are taking place at NRC, not only are removing good people at NRC from the fields in which they are expert, but are discouraging young people from coming into the National Research Council and discouraging young people from careers in science.
What we do at the National Research Council affects far more than the people who are there and the programs that are there. It creates a whole atmosphere. It exacerbates the problem of lack of understanding and lack of support for basic science. We who are leaders in this country have an obligation to give our scientists the freedom to say to the public that science is important, not only for what happens this year and next year but for what happens for the next century in this country and in the world.
We see a total lack of direction. How could the government, in 1986, abolish the Environmental Institute, cut out energy programs, cut out environmental technology and then decide, in 1990, that that is this year's priority. What is likely to happen is that we are going to see the chemistry division turned into an environmental division. What a stupid waste of money. What a stupid waste of people's lives, careers and expertise. How can anybody justify that kind of nonsense?
I want to finish with a few quotes from Canada's most recent Nobel Prize winner. Is it not ironic that in 1986, within the very week that Dr. Polanyi was being named Canada's latest Nobel Prize winner in science, the very lab where he had started his work was being destroyed at NRC. He was not alone. The Basinskis internationally
acclaimed for 30 years for their leading expertise in research which led to developments of tremendous amounts of technology over the years, were having their lab closed down and their lives' work ended.
At that time, Dr. Polanyi was appealing for the National Research Council and for basic research and when talking about his own work stated:
Had they asked whether the research was likely to produce applications and whether those applications would accord with the socioeconomic priorities of the day, they would surely have despaired of our work after a few years.
He talks about how the work which led to his Nobel Prize in 1986 started in 1957, not with the technology, not with an object in mind, but simply because people were seeking basic knowledge that they knew would lead to benefits for humanity as a whole. When asked by a young science student where he should plan his career, Dr.Po-lanyi stated that his advice to a talented and ambitious Canadian scientist would be that he go abroad. Dr.Pola-nyi stated that he did not relish giving him that response, but that at this juncture in our scientific history, which was in the middle of the first round of cuts to NRC, it was the only answer he could give. He also stated that it is not by chance that we talk about research and development. We do not talk about development and research. The research comes first.

However, I want to make a few other comments and I have a few quotations and some figures that might assist my friends opposite in their attempts to make up for five years of neglect and cuts that have damaged one of Canada's foremost scientific institutions.
The National Research Council is clearly one of the most distinguished scientific organizations in this country. Since its founding in 1916, it has been a leader in the scientific field here and abroad. Indeed, out of the National Research Council, as hon. members know, the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited body grew as a result of the research carried on. In addition, the Defence Research Board was a product of that particular council. It has been the foundation stone for contributions to scientific research at Canada's universities, certainly since World War II, and in the period before through its

program of scholarships for promising young Canadian students.
What we have here is an attempt by this government to dismantle, in effect, the National Research Council. The work has been going on in an insidious and carefully manoeuvred way to make it appear that, in fact, nothing is changing. I suggest that it is changing, and all for the worst.
I want to turn to the Prime Minister's comments on this. He has made statements about the government's promises and his hopes for scientific research in Canada. I quote from a statement he made at the University of Waterloo, March 4, 1987: "We are determined that excellence and relevance are the guiding principles for managing our government laboratories. The National Research Council, according to the National Council of Canada, spent $480 million. In this year's Estimates, the 1990-1991 Estimates, the total allowed to the National Research Council is $433 million. That is not only a matter of reduction in the increase in rate, that is an absolute cut in the money available to the National Research Council over a five-year period, five years of cuts by this government in what can only be regarded as one of the jewels in Canada's scientific crown.
Let us look at some of the other things that have gone on in the council. In the good old days, a group of people were appointed to head the National Research Council, and it was made up of a relatively independent group of distinguished men and women, at least half of whom were generally academics, scientists and persons with scientific knowledge of considerable distinction and repute in Canada. Under this government there has
been a shift in the kinds of appointments made to the council. Sixty per cent of the current members are composed of businessmen. It reflects the government's obsession with the bottom line and its unwillingness to consider the importance of scientific research in and of itself and for its own value. I submit that the presence of this particular group on the council is influencing the tenor of scientific research in Canada. It is changing from being pure science to applied research, research which is of interest to a certain group but of no interest to other groups.
In support of that let us look at the recent letter from the president of the National Research Council, Dr. Perron. He said in this letter to the employees dated February 15 of this year:
However, I believe that, even with new resources, we would have an unavoidable obligation to review our activities with a critical eye to scientific merit, relevance to Canada's needs, and to whether NRC is the best place for these activities.
Let us look at those three things. First, a critical eye to scientific merit. Who is putting the critical eye on it? This new board of businessmen. Second, relevance to Canada's needs. From whose perspective? The businessman's perspective, not the scientist's. Third, whether NRC is the best place for these activities. Well, Mr. Speaker, if you had your own lab operating in your own plant and you could get government funding for the lab, would you not rather have the research done there? That is exactly the kind of question that is being faced by the council of the NRC. They have stacked the deck, I suggest, in a way that is unfair to the scientific community of this country.
My colleagues have mentioned the results of what has been going on because of these changes, and I suggest that it is not surprising, given the attitude of the National Research Council as exemplified in this letter. The president's letter continued:
Excellence is essential for all our programs, but excellence is not enough. Our research must also be relevant and mesh well with other NRC activities.
Having made those statements, the embarrassment of having them challenged by other members of the National Research Council, employees, and scientists who are working there was too much. So, an additional memo came out which tells the members of the National Research Council to keep quiet. They were not supposed to talk about it. On February 22, there was a memo to all

March 16, 1990
directors general from Pat Mortimer, Director of the Corporate Secretariat. It read, in part:
-recent media reports have outlined changes that are planned or underway at NRC, and Dr. Perron has sent a letter to employees explaining the context of these decisions, and clarifying the direction NRC is taking.
In the current climate it is preferable to limit the number of people speaking on behalf of NRC. Should there be any further media inquiries on these or related policy issues, the primary spokesperson for NRC will be Dr. Perron or, in his absence, Dr. Ross Pottie.
That is what they said. That is a kind of gag order and I suggest it is inappropriate. What we have here is an attempt to reorganize the National Research Council.
To help my friends, I have a quotation from the time of Nero, A.D. 65, Gauis Petronius Arbiter, Pro-Consul at Bithynia in the Roman Empire. Here is what he said. It is directly relevant to what is going on with the government and its meddling with the NRC today:
We trained hard but it seemed that every time we were beginning to form teams we would be reorganized. I was to learn later in life that we tend to meet every situation in life by reorganizing, and a wonderful method it can be for creating the illusion of progress while producing confusion, inefficiency and demoralization.
We have heard all about the demoralization that is going on at the NRC as a result of the policies being pursued here today.
There is one other scientist I would like to quote, a distinguished physicist at Queen's University, Dr. Alec Stewart. In his speech in November, 1986 to the Bedford Institute of Oceanography he said these words, and I suggest they are relevant to consider in light of the lack of promising future for our young students at the National Research Council and in the scientific community in Canada in general as a result of the cuts that have been going on here. He said:
Any healthy society, especially in lean and straitened times, must look to the future. The injury done in closing laboratories is real but small compared with the more intangible injury and damage done to young people's expectations and to future opportunities for them in Canada. Our perceptive children may see how little we care about the future-their world-and they may reasonably seek the stimulus needed for their growth outside our country.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise as a Minister of State for Industry, Science, and Technology to speak to this opposition motion today.
I have had the chance to listen to a great many of the speeches by hon. members opposite, as well quite factual and helpful speeches by hon. members on this side. I want to make a preliminary comment and then develop further the government's position on not just the National Research Council, but on science and technology funding generally.
I listened carefully this morning until noon and then came back later to listen to more of this debate. Not once did I hear anything from the opposition anything about links to the private sector. Its whole discussion of science and technology reminded me a bit of a defence of a cultural institution. Science and technology, according to the opposition, should go on in universities and government laboratories. Not a word do we hear about feeding and strengthening those institutions through links with the private sector and with the industrial reality of this country. It is a fundamental flaw in everything I have heard from hon. members opposite today. They do not feed the institutions that we have for research and government and university with linkages to the private sector. They do not talk nor care about that. They almost look upon science and technology as a cultural artefact which exists without any linkages to the real world or to the private sector.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite say this is nonsense. It certainly is nonsense but this is what they are saying by neglecting to talk about the links to the private sector. The problem with their approach is they want us to maintain these institutions almost in an incarcerated way, cut off from the lifeblood of what will make them dynamic and strong which is to link them with the real world, industrial research and the private sector.
The government has done a great deal to make sure that happens. Members opposite find this most difficult to agree with, but something we have tried to do is to make them stronger in their linkages with the private sector and the industrial community that is outside of universities and government.
I want to make comments in three different directions. I want to talk about this linkage with the private sector and basic research. I also want to give some examples of how this new approach of linking industrial research that is done in government and universities more with the

March 16, 1990
private sector is bearing fruit and working. I want to delineate how important that is to the government's philosophy toward a stronger scientific and technological sector in Canada.
Let me correct a factual error first. The hon. member for Ottawa West mentioned the cuts of the NRC at the senior management level. She argued that there was an increase in senior management of 13 people. She was contrasting that with decreases in employment in other levels. I want to help her with this. Since November 1989 there has been a reduction of four in executive management at the vice-presidential level in the NRC. I refer her to Part III of the Estimates on page 63.1 will give this to her after I speak today. There has been a reduction in executive and senior management. Therefore, she has either misread the documents or she needed this exegesis of mine of the Estimates. I encourage her to look at page 63 of the Estimates.
The other point is more fundamental. The contribution of the government to science and technology as a proportion of government program spending has gone up under this government over what we inherited. When we came to office, the proportion of federal government spending on programs, as a percentage of federal government spending on programs, was a little over 4 per cent; it is now almost 5 per cent. This is at a time when there are tremendous other pressures, the claimants for government attention are growing, and a time when the government has had to be fiscally responsible. Science and technology has increased in that proportion. That over-all expenditure reality has been overlooked by hon. members opposite and it is very important for me to bring that back into the House so that hon. members will remember what we have done in terms of proving, with dollars and cents, how important science and technology spending is to the government.
Let me just move to some systematic comments about what we are doing. First, the problem with what we have heard today from hon. members opposite is that they are putting the NRC on a kind of Olympian pedestal, and they are doing a disservice to the NRC by doing this. What they want to do is put it on a pedestal. We even had a wonderful quotation from the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. When the hon. member quotes proconsuls from some previous century, I listen carefully. He has good quotations and I like to learn
Government Orders
from them. In his quotation, a quotation against reorganization, he said we should not reorganize because that can be very difficult for the life and health of any institution. I want to address that. If an organization does not change, if it is not renewed, if it does not improve its context in the society of which it is a part, it will die. Those reorganizations are, of course, what we have encouraged and I am going to outline how we have done that.
We should not place this institution on a pedestal, far above the hurly-burly of day-to-day life; we should not do that. What we will do is involve the NRC far more than ever before in the most important challenges facing the nation. We want the NRC to be right at the vanguard of the challenges facing the nation, not to be incarcerated in some ivory tower. We have, in fact, helped that to happen in dozens of ways.
With our support, for example, the NRC's council is sharpening the NRC into one of the country's principal agencies for economic competitiveness. That is something else we have not heard a word about, economic competitiveness. The department of which I am a part is essentially the department in charge of industrial competitiveness. I did not hear a word about competitiveness. What hon. members opposite want to do is protect these institutions from change. I say, if these institutions are going to have strong morale and a sense of purpose, they must deliver on the country's economic competitiveness, and that is what the government has been doing.
The NRC has a very proud history, but it cannot flourish as a monument to past achievements and that is what we have been hearing. Members want this monument to past achievements not to be touched, not to be renewed, and that is not our philosophy. It must always be a national resource, helping to meet the country's most significant needs.
We heard the hon. member for Ottawa West talk about morale. The problem with her presentation was that she linked morale with a kind of glacial stasis. She argued that any change at all will affect morale. She knows that institution well and I do not believe that any institution believes that. Most institutions believe that their morale is improved if the changes made will give a stronger more pertinent long-term future.
March 16, 1990

Government Orders
In looking at history and this quotation of a proconsul from a previous century, it said that we should not reorganize. In fact, the NRC has never been static. It has always gone through waves of pertinent reorganization. Before World War II, the NRC cultivated and supported university science, and this has been brought out during the debate, helping to create world-class faculties out of small undergraduate laboratories. This we acknowledge; this was part of its mission; this was an important contribution, part of its style and essence. During the war, the NRC helped to give the country the technological edge so important to victory in World War II. That was a mission which is different now. It is not participating in that mission, but that was a mission that it had during World War II. That was a change from what went before, and what the NRC is doing today is a change from that.
In the 1950s and 1960s, the NRC undertook fundamental research and used this intellectual fervour to attract and retain for Canada some of the world's best scientific and engineering talent, people like Gerhard Herzberg and John Polanyi, both Nobel Laureates. Recently the NRC has taken up the new challenge, a new development in its distinguished history, to help Canadian industry become the best. Its council is working on a five-year plan that, building on the experience of recent years, will turn the NRC into an engine of applied intelligence. The NRC has always managed to change to better serve this country. The NRC will continue to change, just as the nation as a whole will change.
The NRC has changed. It has gone through, probably, four or five important iterations in its history. The hon. member who quotes the proconsul does not want it ever to change. It is important for its health and its relevance that it goes through these changes. That is what will guarantee its success and its relevance to the country as a whole. We need the NRC. Canada cannot exist without a strong National Research Council. The government is determined to make sure that it does not atrophy by doing things from another era. We are determined to lead, as you know, a competitive renaissance in Canada, and we want the NRC to be part of that.
On the platform of abundant resources, Canada must build right now an edifice of applied intelligence and applied skills in order to maintain our standard of living. We must do that and we cannot be laggards in doing that. Only through economic growth fueled by effective competition in the world's markets can the country maintain its social safety-net, its support for the arts, its regional balance and social harmony. If we are going to win competitively, it requires an intelligent and skilled workforce employing the latest technology. The NRC will be an important way of ensuring that Canada's workforce can be the best. We do not want to incarcerate the NRC and make it irrelevant to the competitive agenda, we want to put them at the forefront of that agenda.
Several things are happening at the NRC to fit it out for its new task. Planning is still taking place, but the next five years will see the following: a renewed commitment to excellence backed by more intensive effort in selected critical areas; closer ties to Canadian industry through participation in consortia, joint research, employee exchanges and increased assistance. I did not hear a word from hon. members opposite about that and how important that is to sustain it and give it a lifeblood of creativity from connections outside of its own doors.
Up until now, government laboratories made extensive efforts to transfer their knowledge to industry. Government laboratories have been very helpful with regard to that. In the new NRC, industry will co-develop that knowledge and the transfer will be to foreign markets in the form of competitive products and services.
Finally, the NRC will resume its role as the finishing school, if you like, for the country's most highly trained scientists and engineers. Once again, the country will enjoy the talents of an NRC alumni of scientific excellence. That is our view of where it is headed. That is our view of its relevance.
Although hon. members opposite do not like to speak of the links with the private sector, yes it is true, the new NRC will be industrially-oriented. It will not be an ivory tower. It will not be an incarcerated institution. We are going to make sure that its roots are strongly in the industrial reality of the country. Its Industry Development Program, like the Industrial Research Assistance Program and the Canadian Institute for Scientific and Technical Information, will be sharpened and honed.

March 16, 1990
Industry will be encouraged to shoulder a larger part of the nation's research, in part by having increased access to the rich talent and the facilities of the NRC. What is wrong with that? Why should we not ask the industry of the country to carry a larger part of this burden? Hon. members opposite too often want to foster dependence on government to an excessive degree. That is not healthy for the country and it certainly is not healthy for the scientific and engineering excellence in this country. If industry is encouraged to shoulder a larger share of the nation's research, in part by having increased access to the rich talent and facilities of the NRC, does this mean that it is any less a laboratory? Are you defiling the laboratory by encouraging it to do this? You are not. You are making the laboratory relevant. Is relevance and usefulness wrong? Of course it is not. Must Canadian technology always be developed by our competitors, instead of our industrial partners? That is our view of the kind of linkages we would like to see for the NRC.
One of the most appalling misunderstandings has been the charge that the new NRC is doing this somehow against its will. I do not believe most members of the NRC are doing this against their will. They do want to have these linkages with the private sector. It is a misunderstanding that somehow this means that they are neglecting basic research.
As a former academic myself, I know what basic research means. I believe that basic research is best conducted not just in an ivory tower. Let me just tell you what is happening about basic research in the NRC. We have had the hon. member for Calgary South speak to this, but we have had some additional information that we think the House should hear.
What do the critics really mean when they talk about this? If they mean that the NRC is neglecting its contribution to humankind store of knowledge, they are wrong. For example, in the Herzberg Institute, the NRC has a world class performer in astronomy. The institute provides Canadian astronomers with first-class facilities, collaboration on frontier research and scientific leadership in important areas.
The NRC is participating, too, in the world-class basic research of 13 of the 16 Centres of Excellence. They are right there and a part of that basic research phenomenon brought by the government, the Centres of Excellence.

to do this. It would like to somehow isolate and incarcerate the NRC. That is not our view.
Canadians, as I have already pointed out, remember with satisfaction the contribution of the NRC in aid of the war effort. The country is in a commercial battle every bit as intensive in its own way today. It is not a military war, but it is a competitive war. We need the NRC to win that battle, and we need it as a vanguard.
If we are to do this, there will be changes in the NRC. Some established programs will be discontinued or handed over to others in the university and industrial sectors. But it will be worth it. The commitment to deficit reduction does not permit the easy solution of endless expansion. Remember, though, the NRC did not establish its Canadian and international reputation by staying the same. That is why it is run by an arm's length council and president, and this is why the council largely sets its own rules and determines its own directions. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister promised us some examples of the products he was talking about and I did not hear of them. I think it betrays his ignorance of NRC if he thinks it was only in the last year or the last few years that links with the private sector have been an important part of NRC's operations. They always have been.
On the other hand, the shift here is to turn away from promoting science to "serving Canada's industrial competitiveness", and you serve Canada's competitiveness by having new products and new technology and most of all from research.
The president of NRC goes on to say that this industrial partnership, this approach on competitiveness, could be temporary and NRC may very well have to shift back to promoting science. When it shifts back it will not have any scientists to do it with. I am shocked that the minister is not concerned about the number of good and competent people we are losing.
I will give him a few examples of why it is important to keep basic research, because that is what international competitiveness is. Before I do so, I want to remind him that he talks about NRC going abroad and selling our technology. We now have 90 per cent of our technology developed abroad and only 10 per cent developed in Canada. It seems to me that the job we have to do is
some work in Canada. We do not do that by cancelling what has led to the science and technology we are now feeding out all over the world. What we learned to do is to enhance that, to make it better, and to improve our ability to develop it here in Canada.
I just want to go back again to the fact that it took 15 years to discover the protein that only grows in tumours and allows us to identify cancer at an early stage. The end result had nothing to do with what people were looking at when they started; they were looking at calcium in tumours. If we cancel that kind of research for five years we are stifling our progressiveness for the next fifty years.
I go back to Dr. Polanyi. The very detectable infrared luminescence that Ken Cashion observed in 1957 led three years later to a suggestion for infrared lasers. A decade later the sort of laser we proposed had become the most powerful source, and yet another decade passed before it began to be evident what the market use might be for such lasers. It was 28 years before the first small observation led to one of the most significant technological developments in the last century. That is what is important. These other things are all products. They are all what you do after you have done the sciences. They are not what you do instead of the sciences. I fail to understand why the minister does not understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to my hon. friend's comments. She gave some very good examples of important contributions NRC scientists have made through basic research to real world success stories, research that was done originally as basic research which lo and behold suddenly became relevant in the real world. That is precisely what we want to do. We do not want to make a total dichotomy between basic science and industrial application. As I made clear in my remarks both must occur.
What I think we have to recognize better than the hon. members opposite have is the link between basic science and real world realities. Let me give some examples of the two happening: the NRC which is a storehouse of basic ideas suddenly becoming adaptable to the real world. For example, the NRC does research on environmental problems. Researchers at the NRC's Biotechnology Research Institute in Montreal are working with Environment Canada on developing new technology to
March 16, 1990

clean up the banks and the sediment in the St. Lawrence River.
Another example of a combination of basic research with the real world, in 1987 NRC scientists identified the mysterious toxin in P.E.I. mussels which caused two deaths and more than 100 cases of serious illness. In Saskatoon, the NRC worked with the University of Saskatchewan to discover a group of chemicals that promote rapid seed germination.
Nothing is more basic to transportation and the life of this country than safe trucks. The NRC is working to make trucks safer and cut down on the number of accidents. For example, when a fuel truck hit a bus in Ottawa last September, I think in the hon. member's riding, killing the truck driver and causing a huge fireball, police turned to NRC experts for help in determining the cause.
Finally I refer to a great example in that we all have to carry bills around in our pockets. NRC technology has made Canadian money counterfeit-proof. I agree with the hon. member. This is basic research adapted marvellously to the realities of the real world. That is what is going to make us competitive and relevant.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to some of the things which the minister has talked about. The minister focused, not surprisingly, in his comments on the essence of the motion itself and the accomplishments of NRC. Incidentally, by noting some of these accomplishments I think the minister is simply proving the point that this is an extremely valuable institution with a fine record behind it, a record which deserves consistent and continuous guaranteed government support so that it has a sense of confidence and security for the future to be able to continue to do the excellent work to which the minister has referred.
One issue which the minister referred to in the earlier stages of his comments is the relationship between research and development and science and technology, on the one hand, and the whole industrial structure on the other hand. Like the minister I think that a fundamental weakness in our society is that economically we do not have in this country what we see in the suburbs surrounding Boston, in the areas surrounding MIT or in
Government Orders
the areas around Stanford in California, that is a massive number of small businesses which have been spun off from the basic research taking place in the universities that have made the connections with industry. By making those connections with industry they have started to make the commitment, as this motion puts it, to promote basic scientific research in Canada as something which is economically significant, economically tight, and economically important.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: What about the University of Waterloo?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
There are exceptions. The University of Waterloo, as the minister suggests, is one which has done relatively well. There are other exceptions. The University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon has done quite well with this kind of thing. Even in those cases we are talking about a level of relationship with the industrial structure which is so different from that which exists in the United States and indeed in many countries in western Europe that we are virtually talking night and day.
What are the reasons for this problem? I have got probably 10 or 11 more minutes in which I can speak, and I want to identify three crucial problems which exist in the heart of our economic structure and help to explain the problem. Often there are people on the Conservative benches, and indeed on the Liberal benches, who wonder why it is that this party is so concerned about foreign ownership and about foreign takeovers in particular. There is a distinction between foreign ownership and foreign takeovers. We can have a new industrial enterprise that when established sets up a number of different parts of its operation, some of which contribute to new scientific activities in this country. When we have foreign takeovers of scientifically based companies, high tech companies, in this country, it is much more difficult to see the likelihood of new expansions in research and development.
I looked at some success stories we have had here in Canada of industries which had recognized the importance of making the link with the scientific community, the university community and institutions like NRC.
I think, for instance, of a company like Mitel or Connaught Labs which grew out of the central core of the University of Toronto. I look at both these institutions and I see now that both of them have been taken

March 16, 1990
Government Orders
over by a foreign owner. As a consequence of foreign ownership, major changes are being undertaken to these high tech companies in Canada which recognized in the past the need for an integral connection between those in industry and those in institutions of scientific research in this country.
Those connections inevitably are destroyed when foreign ownership reduces the staff, through massive rationalization, as in the case of Mitel. It is a polite word for explaining that lots of people are fired and lots of lay-offs take place.
In the case of Connaught Labs we have the key Canadians who turned this enterprise into a successful, high tech enterprise simply eliminated by the French company that has taken it over.
We see the same kind of thing in the case of a company like Federal Pioneer. Federal Pioneer is perhaps the foremost company in this country that develops electrical equipment. For the development of that kind of innovative, electrical equipment, its connections and relationships with the scientific community have been crucial. I am certain those relationships, too, are going to be subject to devastating attack by the foreign takeover which is now to occur with Federal Pioneer. That is one set of issues. I could talk at much greater length about the problems associated with foreign ownership.
The second set of problems are those associated with the free trade arrangement which we have entered into with the United States. I have to talk about two or three examples which have come to my attention in the last year or so, in a particularly compelling and personal way. During the campaign for leadership of the New Democratic Party I worked a good deal of the time in Ontario. One of the places I visited was the massive Massey-Fer-guson plant in Brantford, a plant which strikes you now as perhaps the most symbolic example of the potential consequences of free trade in this country. We have had a free trade agreement in agricultural implements with the United States since 1948. When you go into that magnificent plant in Brantford it is as if you see six full football fields completely bare. That bareness or that destruction is a destruction not just of the jobs, not just of the people and their families, but a destruction of the innovation which was associated with that company. In
fact the major innovation associated with that company has been transferred to the United States, the axial combine which was being produced by Massey.
The same thing is taking place in a company like Stelco, one of the biggest and most important companies in this country. This is a company which has done much research and development. It is now transferring much of its attention to the United States for expansion.
Finally I have to talk about a third area of serious problems, and that is the fact we do not make use of our natural resources to benefit our country, our industrial structure. We see it, for instance, today in the National Energy Board decision which effectively means that we will not be able to apply to exports of natural gas in the future the national interest test that social cost-benefit analysis permitted us to do.
What happens when these three kinds of developments take place? First, we see that there is no longer a focus for scientific research here and for spin-offs from that scientific research. We see it in the case of Mitel. We see it in the case of Massey. We look as well at the destruction of our high tech firms. Those firms are then not able to make the connections which I agree with the minister are so crucial to the ability to establish successful scientific research in the future.
That is why we do not have a commitment to basic research in this country. That is why scientific research is so weak here. It is not because NRC is being attacked, though I agree that the attacks on NRC are foolish and short-sighted. The reason is that the basic policy being followed by this government and the basic policy followed by the previous government was a policy which failed to tackle the questions of foreign ownership and the questions of development of high tech firms of our own, here in this country. That is what we have to change.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Ottawa South which blames the government for not supporting the National Research Council and also for not encouraging basic research.
March 16, 1990

I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that half of the NRC's budget is for applied research, 25 per cent for basic research and 25 per cent for national facilities, CISTI, and administration.
The member who made the motion said this morning that our priorities were to reduce the deficit instead of maintaining funding for research, science and technology in Canada. It is true that we put a lot of emphasis on deficit reduction, Mr. Speaker, but I must tell you that we have to do so now in 1990 because they did not for some 20 years. It is because they too brought down budgets that did not give what they should have for science and technology.
I have some details on that, Mr. Speaker, to tell you about. They say that people do not realize that under the Liberal government, the NRC's budget was $531 million in 1984 and that the forecast for 1986, had the Liberal government remained in power, fell to $480 million.
In 1986, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance made his financial plan for the next five years, of which the last year begins this April 1, he forecast a budget of $3.4 billion, which is nearly $700 million a year. This year, Mr. Speaker, the budget for the last year of this five-year plan is $731 million.
So this means that since 1984 we have been increasing our estimates by 38 per cent each year and if we compare the $3.4 billion figure I mentioned earlier to the $2.3 billion in the Liberal Government Estimates, we have increased the national investment in science and technology by 48 per cent.
I have another statistics, Mr. Speaker. It strikes me that the opposition often suggests we are opening the door to foreign investment here in Canada, we are pushing the door wide open. I have here, Mr. Speaker, three foreign-controlled corporations-Pratt and Whitney, IBM Canada and Imperial Oil. Pratt and Whitney, Mr. Speaker, is investing $243 million a year into research and development, IBM Canada $132 million, and Imperial Oil $54 million.
Government Orders
When they suggest foreign capital is coming here to steal our jobs away, when they suggest as I heard this week that we are selling the Canadian soul away to foreign corporations, I believe this is hogwash and I label that disinformation. This is not information but disinformation Mr. Speaker, because those corporations come here and invest, they come here and do research, they come here and employ our workers and researchers in their operations.
What is wrong with that? What is wrong with that, Mr. Speaker? Why do we have to hear that kind of demagogy, that kind of disinformation about foreign investment?
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if opposition parties were a little more co-operative on government initiatives, they would not accuse us of spending millions of dollars to advertise the budget or the sales tax while that money would be spent for science and technology.
